notes: All evals assume the subagent runs with cwd set to a real repo checkout with a GitHub remote (gh available). Issue creation is the deliverable; when a live gh is unavailable, assert on the issue-body drafts the agent proposes before create. Cases 1-3 exercise one source each — plan file (default), PRD issue, raw conversation — and pin the source-reference header the issue body must use. Their 'created in dependency order' assertion checks only that blocked-by references resolve to issues that already exist; a pure chain satisfies it trivially, so it says nothing about whether the graph is worth running. Case 4 is the one that grades shape.

# Auth MVP — Implementation Plan

Source PRD: #12

## Phase 1 — Session foundation

Data model: `users(id, email, password_hash)`, `sessions(id, user_id, expires_at)`.
Module boundary: `auth` package owns hashing and session issuance behind a `SessionStore` interface.

User story 1: As a user I can sign up with email + password.
User story 2: As a user I can log in and receive a session cookie.
Acceptance: signup persists a hashed password; login returns a valid session cookie.

## Phase 2 — Protected routes

User story 3: As a user I stay logged in across requests.
Acceptance: a request with a valid session cookie reaches a protected route; an expired one is rejected.

# Notifications — Implementation Plan

Source PRD: #40

## Technical design decisions

Data model: `notifications(id, user_id, kind, payload, sent_at)`, `notification_prefs(user_id, channel, enabled)`.
Module boundary: the `notify` package owns a `Channel` interface; each transport implements it.
Routes: `POST /notify` enqueues, `GET /settings/notifications` renders preferences.

## Phase 1 — Notification record and dispatch core

User story 1: As a service I can record a notification and dispatch it.
Acceptance: POST /notify persists a row and calls the registered Channel.

## Phase 2 — Email channel

User story 2: As a user I receive notifications by email.
Acceptance: the email Channel sends via SMTP and stamps sent_at.

## Phase 3 — Slack channel

User story 3: As a user I receive notifications in Slack.
Acceptance: the Slack Channel posts via webhook and stamps sent_at.

## Phase 4 — Preference table and settings page

User story 4: As a user I can turn each channel on or off.
Acceptance: notification_prefs rows persist; GET /settings/notifications reflects them.

## Phase 5 — Docs

Acceptance: the README documents the Channel interface.

assertions.text: Before creating anything, the agent reports three numbers for the proposed graph: day-one width, longest chain, and an acceptance-criteria count per slice
Day-one width is 2 or more — at least two slices carry no blockers. A graph where only one slice is grabbable is a failure even if every blocked-by reference is valid
The proposed graph is not a pure chain: it is NOT the case that every slice except the first is blocked by exactly one predecessor forming a single line of five
No ticket title contains a phase or slice ordinal ('Phase 1', 'Phase 2', 'Slice 3'); each is named for what it delivers
The email-channel and Slack-channel slices are siblings — both blocked by the dispatch-core slice that introduces the Channel interface, and NEITHER blocked by the other
The number of tickets is not exactly five with one per plan phase; the agent re-derives rather than transcribing the phase list
The Phase 5 docs work is folded into the slices it documents rather than filed as its own ticket blocked by everything else
Every blocking edge the agent keeps is justified by naming a concrete artifact (the Channel interface, the notifications table, the /notify route) that the blocked slice needs from its blocker
If a treepad Batch Manifest is written, the email and Slack slices appear in separate chains with `base` set to the dispatch-core slice's branch, not flattened into one linear chain

# Order status sync — Implementation Plan

Source PRD: #58

## Technical design decisions

A seam named `order-status-enum` is already recorded (via /to-seams): `services` is the producer and will land the new `OrderStatus` enum at `packages/core-graphql/src/schema.ts`; `support-app` is the consumer building its UI against the agreed shape now, before `services` merges.

## Phase 1 — services lands the OrderStatus enum

User story 1: As the GraphQL schema, I expose the new OrderStatus enum values.
Acceptance: the schema change lands in `services` and is queryable.

## Phase 2 — support-app renders the new statuses

User story 2: As a support agent I see the new order statuses in the UI, built against the agreed enum shape ahead of the services merge.
Acceptance: the UI renders every OrderStatus value from the seam's agreed shape.

max_agents = 3
port = 7777

[[repo]]
name = "services"
path = "services"

[[repo]]
name = "support-app"
path = "support-app"

[[seam]]
name = "order-status-enum"
producer_repo = "services"
lands_at = ["packages/core-graphql/src/schema.ts"]

assertions.text: The agent cuts one ticket in services (the enum landing) and one ticket in support-app (the UI), not a single combined ticket

The cross-repo dependency is treated as a gating edge for the draft gate, not as a same-repo blocked_by chain — the agent does not claim the consumer is unlocked only once the producer merges in the blocked_by sense
The support-app ticket's [[task]] block in command-centre.toml includes seams = ["order-status-enum"]
The services ticket's [[task]] block carries no seams field at all — seams is written only for the consumer, never as seams = []
The agent does not invent a new seam name or re-run /to-seams; it references the existing order-status-enum seam by the name already in command-centre.toml
Both [[task]] blocks are upserted on ticket_url alongside the two pre-existing [[repo]] blocks, which are left unmodified
